20 J, matching the GPE, so v = 10 m/s.

gold.display: A 0.4 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Assuming no energy losses, calculate its speed just before it lands. (g = 10 N/kg)

steps.say: This is a GPE question, so use \(E_p = mgh\).
Now substitute into m × g × h with g = 10.

steps.hint: Mass times gravity gives the weight, 60 N.

steps.done: That was the whole calculation: 180 J of GPE.

steps.say: We know the energy and want the speed, so rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) to \(v = \sqrt{2E_k \div m}\).
That 36 is v², so take the square root.

steps.done: Rearranging first was the new move here.
Back to 36 J, so v = 6 m/s is right.

steps.say: Two identical bumper cars, same mass. One does 10 m/s. The other does 20 m/s, twice as fast.

steps.pre: How many times faster is the second car? 20 ÷ 10 =

steps.say: Most people guess it carries twice the energy. But kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so we square that factor of 2.

steps.done: So it carries FOUR times the energy, not two.

steps.say: That is exactly why \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\): the speed is squared. Double the speed and you get four times the energy, and four times the crash damage. Squaring the speed is the heart of every energy calculation in this lesson.

opener.prompt: Two identical bumper cars, same mass. One is going 10 m/s. The other is going twice as fast.

steps: Pick the equation: KE = ½mv², GPE = mgh, work W = Fd, or power P = E/t.
Convert units first: mass in kg, height and distance in m, time in s.
Substitute, and for KE square the speed before multiplying.
Calculate, then state the answer with its unit (J or W).
method_card.title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
Four equations do the work here; the skill is choosing the right one.

Kinetic energy \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\): square the speed first. Doubling speed quadruples KE.

GPE \(E_p = mgh\): use vertical height only. This lesson uses g = 10 N/kg.

Work done \(W = Fd\): force times the distance moved.

Power \(P = E/t\): energy per second, in watts. Find the energy first, then divide by time.

steps: Gold problems need two steps: work out the first quantity, then use it in a second equation.
Energy is the usual bridge: find GPE or KE first, then feed that energy into P = E/t, or into a height or speed.
Finish the first calculation fully before starting the second, and carry the exact value across.
gold.title: Gold: two equations chained

example.question: A motor lifts a 50 kg load by 6 m in 10 s. Calculate the power output. (g = 10 N/kg)

steps: Read the question and pick the matching equation: KE = ½mv², GPE = mgh, work W = Fd, or power P = E/t.
The numbers are already in kg, m and s, so substitute them straight in. For KE, square the speed first.
Work it out and write the unit: J for energy or work, W for power.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, straight in

example.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 4 kg trolley moving at 5 m/s.

steps: Sometimes the equation must be turned around first. To find speed from KE, rearrange E_k = ½mv² to v = √(2E_k ÷ m).
Or a value is in the wrong unit: change grams to kilograms (÷ 1000) before you substitute.
Then substitute and solve as usual, keeping the unit on your answer.
silver.title: Silver: convert or rearrange first

example.question: A 0.5 kg ball has 25 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed.

exam_context.frequency: High: energy calculations appear in nearly every physics paper

gold.hint: Find the GPE lost, set it equal to KE, then rearrange for v.
gold.display: A 800 kg rollercoaster car starts from rest at the top of a 45 m drop. Calculate its speed at the bottom, assuming no energy losses. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Energy conserved: GPE lost becomes KE. First \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10.
This 360,000 J is the KE at the bottom. Rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) for v.

guided_steps.hint: Double the energy, divide by mass.

misconceptions.message: Remember to take the square root at the end: v = √900 = 30 m/s, not 900.

gold.hint: Find the KE first, that equals the braking work, then divide by distance for force.
gold.display: A 1,200 kg car travels at 30 m/s. An emergency forces the driver to brake to rest. Calculate the kinetic energy that must be removed by the brakes. Then calculate the average braking force if the car stops in 50 m.

guided_steps.say: First find the KE to remove: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed.
The brakes do this much work. Rearrange \(W = Fd\) to \(F = W \div d\).

guided_steps.hint: Force times distance returns the work.

misconceptions.message: The braking work equals the KE removed. Rearrange W = Fd to F = W ÷ d.

gold.hint: Find the GPE gained, then divide by the time for power.
gold.display: A motor lifts a 120 kg load by 8 m in 6 s. Calculate the power output of the motor in watts. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two steps: GPE gained, then power. \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10.
Now \(P = E/t\): divide by the time.

guided_steps.hint: Power times time returns the energy.

misconceptions.message: GPE = 120 × 10 × 8 = 9,600 J. P = 9,600 ÷ 6 = 1,600 W. Stopping at 9,600 forgets the power step.
Power is P = E ÷ t, not E × t. Multiplying gives 57,600, which is wrong.

gold.hint: Convert grams to kilograms first, then rearrange E = mgh for height.
gold.display: A 500 g ball is launched upwards with 90 J of kinetic energy. Assuming all KE converts to GPE, calculate the maximum height reached. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: All the KE becomes GPE, so \(E_p = mgh\) = 90 J. First convert the mass to kilograms.
Rearrange \(E_p = mgh\) to \(h = E_p \div (mg)\).

misconceptions.message: Convert mass to kg first: 500 g = 0.5 kg. h = E ÷ (mg) = 90 ÷ (0.5 × 10) = 18 m. Leaving mass as 500 gives 0.018 m.
Rearrange E_p = mgh to h = E_p ÷ (mg). Use mass in kg.

gold.hint: Find the GPE gained, then divide by time for power.
gold.display: A 60 kg person climbs stairs, gaining 3 m of vertical height in 4 s. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two steps: GPE gained, then power. \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10.
Now \(P = E/t\).

guided_steps.hint: Power times time returns the energy.

misconceptions.message: GPE = 60 × 10 × 3 = 1,800 J. P = 1,800 ÷ 4 = 450 W. Stopping at 1,800 forgets the power step.

bronze.hint: Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.
bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy uses \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed first.
Now put it into ½ × m × v².

guided_steps.done: E_k = 9 J. Energy is in joules.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 3² = 9. Then E_k = 0.5 × 2 × 9 = 9 J.
Do not forget the half. E_k = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J, not 2 × 9 = 18 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply mass by g by height; g is 10 here.
bronze.display: A 5 kg object is lifted 4 m vertically. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: GPE uses \(E_p = mgh\), with g = 10 N/kg.
That 50 N is the weight. Now multiply by the height.

guided_steps.done: E_p = 200 J. Energy is in joules.

misconceptions.message: Use g = 10 N/kg in this lesson. With g = 10, E_p = 5 × 10 × 4 = 200 J. Using 9.8 gives 196 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply the force by the distance.
bronze.display: A force of 50 N moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done uses \(W = Fd\): force times distance.
Multiply by the distance moved.

misconceptions.message: Work done is force × distance: W = 50 × 3 = 150 J.

bronze.hint: Divide the energy by the time.
bronze.display: A device transfers 600 J of energy in 20 seconds. Calculate its power.

guided_steps.say: Power uses \(P = E/t\): energy divided by time.
Divide by the time in seconds.

guided_steps.done: P = 30 W. Power is in watts.

misconceptions.message: Power is energy ÷ time: P = 600 ÷ 20 = 30 W. Multiplying gives 12000, which is wrong.

bronze.hint: Square the speed, then multiply by half the mass.
bronze.display: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 10 kg skateboard moving at 4 m/s.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed first.
Now ½ × mass × v².

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 4² = 16. Then E_k = 0.5 × 10 × 16 = 80 J.
Do not forget the half: E_k = ½ × 10 × 16 = 80 J, not 10 × 16 = 160 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply mass by g by height.
bronze.display: A 3 kg book falls from a shelf 2 m above the floor. Calculate the GPE it loses. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: GPE: \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10 N/kg.
Multiply by the height fallen.

misconceptions.message: With g = 10, E_p = 3 × 10 × 2 = 60 J. Using 9.8 gives 58.8 J.

bronze.hint: Divide the energy by the time.
bronze.display: An appliance uses 1,500 J in 5 seconds. What is its power?

guided_steps.say: Power: \(P = E/t\).
Divide by the time.

misconceptions.message: P = 1500 ÷ 5 = 300 W. Divide energy by time, do not multiply.

bronze.hint: Multiply the force by the distance.
bronze.display: A horizontal push of 30 N moves a box 4 m along a flat floor. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done: \(W = Fd\).
Multiply by the distance.

misconceptions.message: Work done is force × distance: W = 30 × 4 = 120 J.

silver.hint: Square the speed, then multiply by half the mass.
silver.display: A 1,200 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy gained.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). It starts from rest, so use the final speed. Square it first.
Now ½ × mass × v².

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: v² = 20² = 400. Then E_k = 0.5 × 1200 × 400 = 240,000 J.
Do not forget the half: E_k = ½ × 1200 × 400 = 240,000 J, not 1200 × 400 = 480,000 J.

silver.hint: Rearrange P = E/t to E = P × t.
silver.display: A 500 W motor lifts a load for 12 seconds. Calculate the energy transferred.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange power \(P = E/t\) to find energy: \(E = Pt\).
Multiply by the time in seconds.

guided_steps.done: Dividing back gives 500 W, so E = 6,000 J.
guided_steps.hint: Energy divided by time returns the power.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange P = E/t to E = P × t = 500 × 12 = 6,000 J.

silver.hint: Multiply mass by g by height.
silver.display: A 75 kg person runs up a staircase, gaining a vertical height of 6 m. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: GPE: \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10 N/kg.
Multiply by the vertical height.

silver.hint: Rearrange for v, then remember the square root.
silver.display: A 0.2 kg ball has 10 J of kinetic energy. Calculate its speed.

guided_steps.say: We have energy, we want speed. Rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) to \(v = \sqrt{2E_k \div m}\).
Divide by the mass to get v squared.

misconceptions.message: v² = 2E_k ÷ m = (2 × 10) ÷ 0.2 = 100. Remember to square root: v = √100 = 10 m/s, not 100.

silver.hint: Find the GPE first, then divide by time.
silver.display: A crane lifts a 200 kg beam by 15 m in 30 s. Calculate the power output. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two steps: find the GPE lifted, then the power. Start with \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10.
Now power \(P = E/t\): divide by the time.

misconceptions.message: First find the GPE: 200 × 10 × 15 = 30,000 J. Then P = 30,000 ÷ 30 = 1,000 W. Stopping at 30,000 forgets the power step.

silver.hint: GPE lost equals KE; rearrange for v and square root.
silver.display: A rollercoaster car (mass 600 kg) drops from a height of 20 m. Assuming no energy losses, calculate its speed at the bottom. (g = 10 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Energy is conserved: the GPE lost becomes KE. Find GPE with \(E_p = mgh\), g = 10.
That 120,000 J is now KE. Rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) to find v.

silver.equation_hint: GPE lost = KE gained. Rearrange \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) for v.
